model.label: Tax-funded national health system (SNS) run by 17 regional health services, alongside mutual funds for civil servants that can contract private insurers

overview.statement: Spain's national health system (Sistema Nacional de Salud, SNS) is decentralised and covers the whole population; it is funded mainly from general taxes and covers all residents, including undocumented as well as documented migrants.

Alongside the SNS, two other statutory schemes exist: mutual funds for particular groups (MUFACE for civil servants, MUGEJU for the judiciary and ISFAS for the armed forces), and mutual societies that collaborate with Social Security to cover work accidents and occupational diseases.

The national Ministry of Health handles strategic planning and national regulation, while the health authorities of the 17 regions (autonomous communities) each run their own operational planning, purchasing and resource allocation; the Interterritorial Council of the SNS, made up of the national and regional health ministers, coordinates them.

From 2012 to 2017 entitlement to SNS care depended on a person's legal and employment status; a 2018 law (Royal Decree-Law 7/2018) made residence the basis of entitlement again, restoring full coverage to undocumented migrants. Public coverage is compulsory and people cannot opt out.

A 1986 general health law started Spain's move from a payroll-funded social security system to a tax-funded national health service; the Commonwealth Fund dates the completion of that transition to 1999.

Most primary care is delivered in public health centres, and family doctors act as gatekeepers to outpatient specialist and hospital care; private providers take part mainly in specialist outpatient and hospital services, but public provision meets most health needs.

financing.statement: Public money raised through general taxation is the main source of health funding in Spain: 73.5% of total health expenditure in 2020 and 71.7% in 2021.

locator.section: 3.2 Sources of revenue and financial flows

financing.statement: In 2023 public sources paid for 73% of Spain's health spending (EU average 80%), while households' out-of-pocket payments paid for 21% (EU average 16%).

The SNS is paid for through a decentralised tax system: the regional financing scheme in force since 2011 (approved in 2009) gives most regions a mix of their own taxes, a share of national taxes and transfers, with tax collection shared between the national tax agency (AEAT) and regional tax authorities.

Social security contributions in Spain are earmarked for pensions and other cash benefits, so the tax revenue behind the SNS comes from indirect taxes such as VAT and from direct taxes on income and wealth. Regions collect the taxes fully assigned to them (such as inheritance and property-transfer taxes) and share the revenue of VAT, personal income tax and excise duties.

Under the regional financing law (Law 22/2009), the common-regime regions receive 50% of personal income tax revenue, 50% of VAT revenue and 58% of the excise duties on beer, wine and fermented drinks, intermediate products, spirits, hydrocarbons and tobacco, up from 33%, 35% and 40% under the previous law.
The Basque Country and Navarre have a special fiscal regime: they collect all taxes raised in their territory and pay the central government for the services it provides there, such as defence.

The main transfer to regions, the Guarantee Fund for Basic Public Services (which also covers education and social services), is shared out by a needs formula: population 30%, age-weighted population covered by the SNS 38%, under-17s 20.5%, people aged 65 and over 8.5%, plus land area, population density and insularity. It is financed with 75% of the regions' tax revenue plus a central government contribution.

The civil servants' mutual funds (MUFACE, ISFAS and MUGEJU) are paid for by a mix of payroll contributions and public transfers, and the mutual societies covering work accidents and occupational diseases are paid for by employers' contributions.

locator.section: 3.2 Sources of revenue and financial flows

financing.statement: Mutual-fund members pay a monthly contribution of EUR 20 to 50 depending on their civil-service grade, regardless of how many dependants are covered; members' contributions cover up to 15% of the funds' spending and the other 85% comes from the national budget, funded mainly from income tax.

MUFACE's 2025-2027 contract with the insurers Adeslas and Asisa has a total budget of EUR 4,808.5 million, EUR 1,276.5 million more than the previous contract, and raises the weighted average premium paid to insurers by a cumulative 41.2% over its three years, with premiums now rising by age band.

Voluntary health insurance paid for 6% of health spending in 2023 (EU average 4.5%); it is used both to get faster specialist and hospital care and to cover services outside the SNS package, such as some dental care.

About one in five people in Spain hold voluntary health insurance on top of public coverage; the covered share rose from 15.8% of the population in 2015 to 20.8% in 2021, and at the end of 2022 policies bought by employers made up 29.8% of premiums and 34.1% of people insured.

Private health insurance gets tax advantages, which vary by region: the self-employed can deduct premiums from taxable income, employees can deduct premiums their employer pays up to EUR 500 per covered person a year (EUR 1,500 for a person with a disability), and health insurance premiums are exempt from VAT and from the insurance premium tax.

WHO notes that, unlike most EU governments, Spain's government subsidises some buyers of private health insurance through the tax system, and that when the 2021 budget raised the insurance premium tax from 6% to 8%, health insurance was left out of the increase.

Out-of-pocket payments were 20.6% of total health spending in 2021; household spending on health, as measured by the national household budget survey, grew from EUR 17,859 million in 2015 to EUR 23,379 million in 2022, equal to 3.9% of household budgets.
According to the Ministry of Health's public health spending statistics (EGSP), public spending on health reached EUR 101,739 million in 2024, 4.2% more than in 2023 and equal to 6.4% of GDP.
Regional governments accounted for 93.6% of public health spending in 2024.

locator.section: Gasto en el sector de las comunidades autónomas

financing.statement: EU money also funds health in Spain: Spain assigned EUR 2.4 billion (1.5% of its Recovery and Resilience Plan) to health, and EU Cohesion Policy funds for 2021-27 allocate a further EUR 1.1 billion.

covered.statement: The SNS basic package, free of charge, covers all prevention, diagnosis, treatment and rehabilitation services plus emergency medical transport, including primary care, mental health, palliative care, basic dental services, specialist outpatient and inpatient care, home care and organ transplants.
The main gaps in the public package are dental care, which is limited and varies between regions, and optical care, which is not publicly covered.

locator.section: Box 3.1 What are the key gaps in coverage?

covered.statement: Regions may add services to their own package beyond the common SNS package, but only if they can show they can pay for them within budget-stability rules and inform the Interterritorial Council.

An 'accessory' package of non-essential services that could carry co-payments was created during the 2012 austerity reforms but had never been regulated as of June 2024; a draft universality law then before Parliament would return to a single benefits package.

Who decides coverage: new benefits are added by the Interterritorial Council of the SNS, on proposals from its Commission on Benefits, Insurance and Financing, after compulsory technical advice from the Spanish network of health technology assessment agencies.

For medicines, after marketing approval a company may seek public reimbursement; the Interministerial Commission on Medicine Prices, an advisory body of the Ministry of Health, decides using criteria including disease severity, the needs of particular groups, therapeutic and social value and cost-effectiveness, budget impact, cheaper alternatives and degree of innovation.

A national medicines evaluation network created in 2020 added economic evaluation to the therapeutic positioning reports that inform drug pricing and reimbursement, but a national court struck that economic evaluation down in July 2023 after a lawsuit by the Spanish pharmaceutical industry association.

Dental and optical coverage is being widened: in June 2024 EUR 68 million was set aside for oral health aimed at children under 14, pregnant women, people with disabilities and people with cervical or facial cancer, and the SNS was due to be able to fund glasses and contact lenses for children from low-income families from the last quarter of 2025.
Public employees in the mutual funds are the only people with a real choice between public and private coverage, and about 79% of them choose private coverage.

Under MUFACE's 2025-2027 contract the two private insurers were to cover 734,000 members and 280,000 dependants, out of 1,014,692 people; the rest of MUFACE's roughly 1.5 million people had opted for the public system.
The 2025 MUFACE contract added a second yearly window, in June as well as January, in which members can switch between the public system and the private insurers or between insurers.

cost_sharing.statement: As of 2023 there were no user charges for primary care, outpatient visits, diagnostic tests, inpatient care, inpatient medicines or emergency care.

cost_sharing.statement: For most outpatient prescription medicines, patients pay a percentage of the price that depends on income and status (2023): pensioners pay 10% if their income is under EUR 100,000 and 60% above it; mutual-fund members pay 30%; other people pay 40% with income under EUR 18,000 and 50% with income of EUR 18,000-100,000.

cost_sharing.statement: Most medicines for chronic conditions carry a 10% co-payment capped at EUR 4.24 per item, a cap updated each year for inflation (2023).

cost_sharing.statement: Pensioners outside the mutual funds have a monthly cap on prescription co-payments linked to income (2023): EUR 8.23 with income under EUR 18,000, EUR 18.52 with EUR 18,000-100,000, and EUR 61.75 above EUR 100,000.

cost_sharing.statement: Medicines given in hospital outpatient departments for a set of serious conditions that need hospital diagnosis or close follow-up, such as cystic fibrosis, multiple sclerosis, hepatitis C, HIV, oral chemotherapy and rheumatoid arthritis, carry no co-payment.

cost_sharing.statement: Orthoprosthetic devices have no overall spending cap; instead each item has its own cap, from EUR 0 to EUR 36, that does not depend on income.

cost_sharing.statement: Exemptions have widened since 2020: people receiving the guaranteed minimum income were exempted from co-payments in 2020, and in 2021 full exemption was extended to low-income pensioners, children with moderate or severe disabilities and households receiving child benefits.
The co-payment exemptions introduced in 2020 and 2021 benefited 7.3 million people in 2024.
Households paid for one third of retail pharmaceutical spending in 2023; public funds covered the other two thirds (67%).
Households pay out of pocket mainly for dental care (32% of out-of-pocket spending), outpatient medicines (24%) and optical care.

financial_hardship.statement: In WHO's analysis of household budget surveys for 2006-2019, catastrophic health spending was concentrated among the poorest fifth of households, and almost all of its increase over the period came from a large rise in that poorest fifth.

Over 2006-2019 the households facing catastrophic health spending shifted from those headed by older and retired people towards those headed by working-age people (aged 35-50), employed and unemployed people, and couples with children.

Dental care and medical products drive catastrophic spending in every income group, mainly because the SNS largely excludes dental and optical care, especially for adults; among the poorest fifth, co-payments for outpatient medicines also contribute.

WHO found catastrophic spending in Spain much lower than its heavy reliance on out-of-pocket payments would suggest, which it attributes to the design of SNS coverage and the strongly redistributive effect of public health spending.
WHO's review warned that waiting times for medical examinations and specialist care can cause financial hardship and unmet need and widen socioeconomic inequalities in access.

additional_care.statement: Long-term care took 10% of current health expenditure in 2023, well below the EU average of about 18%, and preventive care took 3% (EU average 4%).
Long-term care is run by the regions; the autonomous communities fund 64% of it, cost sharing 21% and the national government 15%.

The 2006 Dependency Act set up the System for the Assistance of Dependent People (SAAD), which offers personal care, home support and financial help for caregivers, with eligibility and co-payments based on the level of dependency and income.
Residential elderly care is mostly private: only 25% of care home places are publicly owned, and some of those are privately managed.
Private long-term care insurance is small: 163,752 people held it in 2022, about 0.4% of adults.

In April 2025 the Interterritorial Council approved a Mental Health Action Plan for 2025-27 with EUR 101 million, aimed at more rational use of psychotropic drugs, the shortage of mental health professionals, and human rights and dignity.

access.statement: Among people who needed medical care in 2024, 2.6% reported unmet needs because of cost, waiting lists or travel distance (EU average 3.6%); among those at risk of poverty the rate was 2.3% (EU average 6.0%).
Unmet needs are much higher for dental care: in 2024, 9.3% of people needing dental care reported unmet needs (EU average 6.3%), rising to 22.1% among those at risk of poverty (EU average 13.6%).
Unmet needs for mental health care more than doubled after 2021: in 2024, 7.9% of survey respondents in Spain said they had forgone mental health care, close to the EU average of 7.2%.

On 31 December 2025, 853,740 patients were waiting for elective surgery in the SNS, with an average wait of 122 days, four days less than a year earlier (figures as corrected by the Ministry of Health).
At the end of 2025, 21.6% of patients on the surgical waiting list had been on it for more than six months, 1.3 points fewer than a year earlier.

Five procedures (heart valve surgery, coronary bypass, cataract, hip and knee replacement) have a guaranteed maximum wait of 180 days in the SNS. At the end of 2025 hip replacement averaged 98 days and knee replacement 105 days, and 13.7% and 15.9% of those patients respectively had waited longer than the maximum.
On 31 December 2025, 84.42 people per 1,000 were waiting for a first hospital specialist appointment; their average wait was 102 days, and 61.5% had been given an appointment more than 60 days away.

In the 2023 Health Barometer survey, 38.2% of respondents had waited more than three months from a family doctor's referral to a specialist appointment, and 69.8% said getting a family doctor appointment took more than 24 hours, with an average wait of nine days.
The share of hip replacement patients waiting more than three months rose from 38% in 2019 to 68% in 2020 and fell to 44% in 2024, still above the pre-pandemic level.
Staff are unevenly spread across regions: in 2022 primary care doctors ranged from 0.6 to 1.1 per 1,000 people and primary care nurses from 0.5 to 0.9 per 1,000.
Patients can choose a family doctor, but in practice only within the same primary care team and subject to limits on how many patients each doctor may register.

In an industry survey (EFPIA's Patients W.A.I.T. indicator) cited by the profile, medicines approved by the EU in 2020-2023 took on average 616 days to be publicly reimbursed in Spain, 7% longer than the EU average of 578 days, but 71% of them were covered as of January 2025, against an EU average of 46%.

outcomes.statement: Life expectancy at birth in Spain was 84 years in 2024, 2.3 years above the EU average and the third highest in the EU after Italy and Sweden.
In 2022 Spain had among the lowest avoidable mortality rates in the EU: 124 deaths per 100,000 people from preventable causes and 62 per 100,000 from treatable causes.
In 2023, 30-day mortality after hospital admission was 8.0 per 100 patients for heart attack (EU average 8.4) and 12.6 per 100 for ischaemic stroke (EU average 13.1).
Cancer screening uptake in 2023 was 69% for breast cancer (women 50-69) and 68% for cervical cancer (women 20-69), above EU averages, but only 43% for colorectal cancer.
In the GBD 2019 study, Spain's Healthcare Access and Quality (HAQ) Index score for ages 0-74 was 89.7 (95% uncertainty interval 87.2-91.4) in 2019, 18.6 points higher than in 1990.

outcomes.statement: In the OECD PaRIS survey of people aged 45 and over with chronic conditions (2023-24), 85% of Spanish respondents rated the quality of their care as good and 85% found the system person-centred, similar to the average of the 10 EU countries reporting.

costs.statement: Spain spent 9.2% of GDP on health in 2023, slightly below the EU average of 10.0%.
Health spending per person in Spain was EUR 3,137 in 2023, about one fifth below the EU average.
By function, 36% of health spending went on outpatient care and 27% on inpatient care in 2023, while outpatient medicines and medical devices took 21%.
Retail pharmaceutical spending per person was EUR 472 in 2023, 7% below the EU average of EUR 510 after adjusting for purchasing power.

Medicines dispensed in hospitals are a growing part of drug spending: by 2023 the retail share had fallen to 72% and the hospital share had risen to 28%, and inpatient-sector pharmaceutical spending was EUR 9.6 billion in 2023, up 8% (after 4.8% growth the year before).
Medicine prices in Spain are set by a specific methodology rather than by the market; in 2024 the Ministry of Health revised the prices of more than 17,000 medicines to save EUR 139 million.

Generics made up 47% of medicines dispensed by community pharmacies (by units) in 2024, about the same as the 48% of 2014; the profile notes that reference pricing keeps the price gap between generics and brands small.
Health took 14.5% of total government spending in 2023, almost unchanged from 14.4% in 2019.
Public health spending per person differed widely between regions in 2024, from EUR 2,332 in the Basque Country and EUR 2,322 in Asturias to EUR 1,658 in Andalusia and EUR 1,779 in Madrid.

what_works.statement: Spain's rates of avoidable hospital admissions, especially for congestive heart failure and diabetes, are among the lowest in the EU, which the profile attributes partly to strong primary care that provides continuity and limits fragmentation of specialist care.

Deaths from treatable conditions fell over the past decade, including during the COVID-19 pandemic; the profile credits prioritisation after the lockdowns, when urgent heart disease and cancer cases were fast-tracked.

WHO lists as strengths that SNS entitlement rests on residence, with undocumented migrants entitled to the same coverage as residents; that the benefits package is broad and varies very little between regions; and that health centres are evenly spread across the country.
Spain had the world's highest rate of deceased organ donation; in 2021 it transplanted 4,781 organs, the second-highest rate per million people in the world after the United States.

Core features of Spain's donation and transplant programme include a three-tier governance structure, close working relations with the media, dedicated professional roles, comprehensive reimbursement of donation activity and intensive tailored training for all staff.
Informal payments do not appear to be a problem in Spain; Eurobarometer surveys consistently place it among the EU countries with the lowest self-reported informal payments.

problems.statement: Remaining access gaps include administrative hurdles to obtaining the guaranteed minimum income (on which co-payment exemption depends), limited coverage of services such as dental and optical care, and long waiting lists and treatment delays; the profile calls waiting times the major barrier to access in Spain.
Working-age people have no cap on prescription co-payments, which may stop people on lower incomes from getting outpatient prescriptions.

In publicly funded surgery in Catalonia (2015-2019), middle-income patients waited 2-6 fewer days than low-income patients for hip replacement, cataract surgery and hysterectomy, and less than a day fewer for breast cancer surgery; the gaps arose within hospitals and were not explained by patient or hospital characteristics.

Private insurance is concentrated among the better-off: holders tend to be aged 31-60, employees of large companies and members of richer households, and in 2019 about 40% of households in the richest fifth had it against 10% in the poorest fifth.

WHO recommended reviewing the efficiency and equity of tax subsidies for private health insurance, which mainly benefit richer households, and of letting mutual-fund members opt for private provision, saying both policies widen inequalities in access.
The medical workforce is ageing: 43% of doctors were 55 or older in 2022, which the profile says points to retirement waves that will add to existing pressures.
Spain had 5.9 nurses per 1,000 people in 2023, below the EU average of 8.5, though the figure leaves out nurse assistants and other support roles and so understates the nursing workforce.
Decisions on drug approval and pricing are made by the Ministry of Health while the regions pay for all pharmaceutical care, a split that causes tension between them.
Growing waiting times, notably in primary care, have increased the public's sense that access to the health system has weakened, which may widen inequalities between the better-off and the worse-off.
Antibiotic use has risen again since 2021, reaching 24.1 defined daily doses per 1,000 people in 2023 against an EU average of 19.9, which may put the 2030 reduction target at risk.

reforms.statement: In 2024 the Interterritorial Council approved the Primary and Community Care Action Plan 2025-27 to build primary care workforce capacity, improve working conditions, have regions plan to retain staff and promote continuity of care.

In June 2024 Spain launched a public health surveillance network covering five domains, and in July 2025 it created a State Public Health Agency as a central authority for anticipating and managing public health challenges.

A broad draft Law on Medicines and Health Products, opened to public consultation in April 2025 and still awaiting Parliament, seeks to update Spain's medicines legislation; its goals span fairer access, sensible use of medicines, environmental impact, public scrutiny, digitalisation and consistency with EU law.

The draft medicines law sets procedures for conditional, early and temporary public funding of medicines with special added value for particular groups while a final funding decision is pending, which the profile expects to speed access to innovative therapies.
On 12 May 2026 the Council of Ministers approved, in a second reading, the bill on Public Management and Integrity of the SNS and sent it to Parliament.
The bill makes direct public management the preferred way of providing SNS care and repeals Law 15/1997, which had opened the way to new forms of private management of the public system.
The bill would ban contracts in which a private company both builds health facilities and manages the care provided in them.

Valencia has reversed public-private partnerships for running health areas in four of the five places it used them: Alzira (2018), Torrevieja (2021), Denia (January 2024) and Manises (May 2024); it planned to keep the Elx-Vinalopó contract on yearly extensions after it ended in 2025.
To train more doctors, public universities offered 677 new medical student places in 2023/24, raising first-year places by 12%, with EUR 52 million from the national government.

A 2023 technical document set 13 criteria for hard-to-fill posts; a primary care post meeting at least five qualifies for incentives such as extra pay, housing support, career development and better work-life balance.
In April 2024 the SNS set up a Working Group on Waiting Lists to end differences between regions in how waiting lists are managed and recorded.

us_lessons.statement: For countries reforming transplant systems, the review cautions against overrating presumed-consent laws: in Spain donation goes ahead only after consulting the family and with its approval, and the authors conclude legislation must be backed by working protocols that the public and professionals accept.

Spanish hospitals receive budget funding for donation costs based on their past donation rates, and the review advises countries reforming their transplant systems to examine their own reimbursement rules for financial barriers to donation.

Spain's three-tier governance structure for donation is seen as a major reason for its success and has been used as a model by other European programmes, including those of the United Kingdom, Portugal and Italy.

The review suggests countries reforming their transplant systems could adopt the core features of the Spanish model and should also support living donation, which it identifies as an area where Spain itself could improve.
